name: Face tanning for 'glow'
lead: Face tanning for glow means warming or deepening facial skin tone, through sun or tanning-bed exposure or through sunless products such as DHA self-tanners, gradual-tan moisturizers and bronzers, so that the face looks healthier, more even and more defined. Looksmaxxing forum users use it to counter a pale or washed-out look, to soften visible redness and to make cheekbones and jaw read with more shadow and contrast.[1][8][9]

Sunless methods are the most discussed. Wikipedia describes DHA as reacting with amino acids in the outer dead skin layer, with colour fading over roughly 3 to 10 days, and bronzers as temporary tints that wash off and are used for one-day colour or to complement a DHA tan.[1][11] Forum threads cover facial self-tanner choices, avoiding an orange or patchy result, and using bronzer with contouring to change how the face's structure looks.[8][9][10]

Research relevant to the topic includes a nationwide survey of sunless tanning product users, studies of tanning behaviour and skin-tone preferences, and perception experiments in which faces with added carotenoid (yellow-golden) colouration were rated more attractive than faces with matched melanin (tan) colouration, although both were preferred to paler versions.[2][4][18][19] Patent filings describe cosmetic compositions designed to give a tan or glow with less streaking.[5][6][7]

angle.text: A tan or bronzer changes the colour and contrast of facial skin right away or over a day or two. Community members use it to even out tone, mask redness and add shadow along cheekbones and jaw.

infobox: About 3-10 days (DHA); spray tans about 5-10 days [1]
FDA approves DHA for external use, not eyes, lips, mucous membranes or inhalation [1]
Self-tanner, bronzer, contouring, gradual tanner, sunbeds

paras: A tan changes the colour, contrast and apparent health of facial skin. People describe the effect as warmer undertone, less visible redness and under-eye shadow, and more definition along the cheekbones and jaw, because darker skin gives more tonal contrast between lit and shaded planes of the face.[1][10] The practice sits between skincare and makeup: sunless products are applied like a lotion or mousse, and bronzers like a cosmetic.[11]
The goal can be a lasting base colour (DHA tanner, gradual tanner or salon spray tan) or a same-day finish (bronzer), and many people combine them, using bronzer to complement a DHA tan.[1][11]

Sun and tanning beds darken skin through UV-driven melanin production. Wikipedia explains that UVA quickly oxidises existing melanin, giving a fast but short-lived darkening, while UVB triggers new melanin production, appearing two or three days after exposure and lasting weeks or months.[16] Sunless options include DHA-based self-tanners in creams, mousses, drops and sprays, salon spray tans, gradual-tan moisturizers and wash-off bronzers.[1][11]

Bronzers are makeup-like products that tint the surface and come in powders, gels, lotions and sprays; they are used for colour on the day or on top of a DHA tan. Common ingredients include walnut oil extract, jojoba extract and caramel, and some lotions contain a gradual tanning agent so colour builds with repeated use.[1][11] Wikipedia notes that application errors can leave colour looking orange and patchy, and that bronzers may rub off onto clothing.[11]

DHA is not a dye and does not involve melanin; it reacts with amino acids in the dead outer skin layer and the colour fades as that layer sheds, over about 3 to 10 days. Erythrulose works similarly but develops more slowly. Wikipedia lists contact dermatitis as a possible reaction to either agent.[1]

Carotenoids such as lycopene, beta-carotene and canthaxanthin can change skin colour when consumed in high amounts, a harmless effect that fades over months; Wikipedia reports that high doses of synthetic beta-carotene have been linked to higher lung cancer rates in smokers and that canthaxanthin pills have been linked to hepatitis and yellow retinal deposits.[1] Unlicensed melanotan products are sold online and in some salons, and health agencies have warned against them since 2007.[1]

Before the 1920s in the United States and Western Europe, a tan was associated with outdoor labourers and pale skin with higher status. According to Wikipedia, sunlight was promoted as a health remedy in the early 1900s, and in the 1920s Coco Chanel's tan after a Riviera cruise and singer Josephine Baker's popularity helped make tanned skin fashionable; Jean Patou launched the first sun tan oil in 1927.[16]

DHA's skin-staining effect was noticed in the 1950s by Eva Wittgenstein at Cincinnati Children's Hospital when an oral treatment stained skin brown. Man-Tan (1959) and Coppertone's QT (1960) were early products, and their orange tone harmed the category's image. Reformulations and, from the late 1990s, automated spray-tan booths expanded the market.[1][11] Friedrich Wolff developed the sunbed in 1975 and tanning beds reached the US in 1978; by 2007 the US indoor tanning industry was estimated at five billion dollars a year.[16][17]

Patent documents describe compositions in which a tanning agent is combined with a cationic copolymer to intensify colour and reduce streaking.[5][6][7] Wikipedia cites a 2019 Google Trends analysis showing rising US interest in sunless tanning relative to tanning beds.[1]

Forum users discuss facial self-tanner brands, how to avoid missed spots around the eyes and hairline, and ways to correct patchiness; one user describes fixing an uneven application with an exfoliating scrub, and another opens a thread after missing areas around the eyes, mouth and hairline and ending up orange in places.[8] Other threads ask how to tan without looking fake on medium skin, whether tanning looks better on lighter skin, and whether darker-skinned users benefit from bronzer.[12][13][14]

One thread argues that bronzer and contour can "change your entire face", reflecting a view that darkening and shading the face alters its apparent structure.[10] Another thread discusses pale skin versus a tan in the context of well-known looksmaxxing personalities.[9]

In the Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, Lefevre and Perrett (2015) altered faces to be high or low in carotenoid or melanin colouration across three studies. Both higher carotenoid and higher melanin colouration were rated more attractive than lower levels, carotenoid colouration was preferred when levels were matched, and the carotenoid preference was stronger for female faces than male faces. The authors suggest that because men naturally have darker skin, melanin may enhance masculinity.[18]

A 2019 cross-cultural follow-up by Ip, Lewis and Lefevre used Caucasian and Hong Kong Chinese participants and found that high carotenoid colouration was preferred in faces and body parts but not in scrambled control stimuli.[19] The 2016 survey of 399 young Asian Australians found that preferring a darker skin tone, along with acculturation to Australia, was significantly linked to tanning, with over 35% reporting outdoor tanning and over 10% solarium tanning.[4]

Wikipedia reports the FDA has approved DHA for external use but not around eyes, lips, mucous membranes or for inhalation. A 2007 study led by Katinka Jung found more free radicals formed after sun exposure in DHA-treated skin, a 2004 cell study reported DHA induced DNA damage and cell-cycle block, and a 2010 opinion of the European Commission's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety concluded DHA spray tanning posed no risk, a conclusion criticised by specialists who noted much of the evidence came from industry-linked unpublished studies. Wikipedia advises sun protection for a day after application and notes that the sunscreen in some tanners fades quickly.[1]

A nationwide German telephone survey of 3,000 people aged 14 to 45 found 7.5% had used sunless tanning products in the past year, with higher use among tanning-bed users (16.1%) than people who had never used beds (5.8%); the authors warned that a fake tan may lead people to overestimate their natural skin type and expose themselves to too much UV, and noted lower UV-risk awareness among users.[2] A letter from Irish dermatologists reported that fake tan on skin complicates dermoscopy in pigmented lesion clinics.[3]

UV tanning is linked to skin cancer risk: the WHO classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen, and Australia banned commercial tanning beds in 2015.[17] Wikipedia also cites a 2010 study linking frequent tanning-bed use to a tripled risk of melanoma.[16]

No trials were found testing face tanning specifically for perceived glow or redness masking. Related studies include user surveys of sunless tanning products and tanning behaviour,[2][4] image-based perception experiments on carotenoid and melanin skin colouration,[18][19] a nursing-student study of 217 participants finding no significant difference in hand-hygiene lotion removal between fake tan wearers (21%) and non-wearers,[15] and a 2011 study cited on Wikipedia in which a carotenoid-based golden skin tone was rated more attractive and healthy-looking than a suntan.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, facial self-tanner and bronzer are discussed as quick tone and contrast tools, with much of the conversation about avoiding an orange or uneven result.[8][12]

claims.claim: Bronzer and contour can change the apparent structure of the whole face
claims.believers: One thread's author argues that bronzer plus contour reshapes how the face reads.[10]
claims.experts: No published study has tested bronzer contouring for perceived facial structure.

claims.claim: A fake tan makes pale skin look healthier
claims.believers: Users say a tan hides pallor and redness and adds contrast, and they trade brand recommendations.[9][8]
claims.experts: In perception experiments, faces with higher melanin or carotenoid colouration were rated more attractive than paler ones; no trial tested self-tanner for this.[18]

claims.claim: A golden, carotenoid look beats a deep tan
claims.believers: Proponents of facial glow describe the aim as a warm, healthy-looking tone rather than a dark tan.
claims.experts: Lefevre and Perrett found carotenoid colouration preferred over matched melanin colouration, especially for female faces; a 2019 cross-cultural study found carotenoid colouration preferred in faces in Caucasian and Hong Kong Chinese samples.[18][19]

claims.claim: Self-tanner looks natural on some skin tones and not others
claims.believers: Threads ask whether fake tan works better on white than non-white skin and how to avoid an artificial look on medium skin.[13][12]
claims.experts: No studies compare results across skin tones.

claims.claim: Sunless tan is a safer alternative to UV tanning
claims.believers: Users treat self-tanner as a way to get colour without sun exposure.[8]
claims.experts: The nationwide survey notes sunless products are seen as a healthy alternative to sunbathing but may be linked to risky tanning behaviour; Wikipedia says a sunless tan does not protect against UV.[2][1]

claims.claim: Streaks and orange tone are the main hazard of facial self-tanning
claims.believers: Users report missed spots around the eyes, hairline and mouth leaving orange or patchy results, and discuss correcting them with exfoliation.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that application errors can leave colour orange and patchy.[11]

card.summary: Bronzer or tan to hide redness and look healthy; sunless products are temporary and give no UV protection.
card.note: UV tanning is linked to skin cancer; sunless tans do not protect from UV.

quick.overview:
People darken facial skin to look healthier or hide redness, using sun or tanning beds, or sunless products such as DHA self-tanners and bronzers.

Sunless products fade over days. Studies specifically testing face tanning for glow were not found.
quick.mechanism: DHA reacts with amino acids in the skin's dead outer layer to produce a brown colour without UV. Bronzers are surface pigments that wash off.
quick.risks: UV tanning is associated with skin cancer risk. Sunless products can cause contact dermatitis, are not approved for eyes, lips or inhalation, and give no UV protection.
